81.0.0.en: 1- Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob.

81.0.1.en: 1- The psalm calls God's people to express their love for the mighty God, who supported His people and saved them with great power, and who is the only strength of the people that relies on Him. So it does not lean on weapons, or its own human strength, or its relations with strong surrounding nations; all this is nothing before the power of God. This singing declares the faith of the people and establishes them in it, and even gives them joy, delight, and fellowship with God.

81.0.2.en: 2- From much singing to God the hearts of the people were filled with joy, so the psalm called them to shout aloud, because shouting is loud voices showing the heart's attachment to God, and they sing to the God of Jacob, because Jacob relied on God, so Esau was not able to harm him, but on the contrary the two brothers embraced in love (Gen 33:4). So the people shout to God, their mighty God who protects them and keeps them.

81.1.0.en: 2- Raise a song, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant lute with the rebab.

81.1.1.en: Timbrel: a wooden frame over which a thin skin is stretched, and on the sides of the frame there are small cymbals to give strong sounds for keeping rhythm. To play it one strikes the stretched skin with the hand, and it is now called the "riqq".

81.1.2.en: Lute: a stringed musical instrument known to this day by the same name, consisting of a wooden box over which a number of strings are stretched.

81.1.3.en: Rebab: plural of rababa, a stringed instrument over which twelve strings are stretched and it is played with the fingers, or with a plectrum like the lute.

81.1.4.en: The psalm calls the praising people to sing to God with high notes, accompanied by musical instruments such as the lute, the timbrel and the rebab, to express joy and to praise God who gives them victory over their enemies, especially since the people had been accustomed to singing with musical instruments since their departure from the land of Egypt, when Miriam led the people in their praise and glorification.

81.2.0.en: 3- Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, at the crescent, for the day of our feast. 4- For this was a statute for Israel, and a law of the God of Jacob.

81.2.1.en: Trumpet: a musical instrument resembling the horn of an animal, with a narrow opening at one end and wide at the other, and it is blown for playing.

81.2.2.en: The psalm also calls the people to use trumpets, and it was the priests who blew the trumpets, for blowing the trumpet is a priestly work, because the trumpet is a symbol of the word of God. And trumpets are used at the new moon, at the appearing of the crescent, and at the Feast of Trumpets which is the head of the seventh month, and is the beginning of the year. It calls people to repentance and a new beginning, and reminds them of the power of God that gave them victory over their enemies, so it fills the hearts of the people with zeal to begin a strong spiritual life with God. And blowing the trumpets is a divine command, and a statute that God's people fulfilled at the head of every month to renew feelings of repentance, hope and strength. And the Church holds prayers and Liturgies at the head of the year, to call her people to repentance and hope.

81.3.0.en: 5- This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out over the land of Egypt. I heard a language that I knew not:

81.3.1.en: 1- God made the feast, meaning all the religious feasts, in which trumpets and spiritual memorials are used, a testimony in the midst of His people, declaring their faith in God and their worship of Him. And he chose the name Joseph as a symbol of all God's people; because Joseph was the cause of bringing his brothers into the land of Egypt and honoring them, but the Egyptians enslaved them and humiliated them after this, and so the children of Israel lived as slaves among the Egyptians, who have a language that God's people do not know, but their consolation was their knowing God, and God's knowing them, which was manifested in the religious feasts and seasons, and in every worship they offered to God.

81.3.2.en: 2- Joseph is a symbol of Christ, for Christ bears witness through Joseph in the land of Egypt to the work of God; because Joseph was sold as a slave, and bore sufferings for thirteen years, and then was raised to the throne of Egypt, and Christ became incarnate, and took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and bore sufferings, and was obedient unto death, even the death of the Cross, and then rose in great glory, conquering all the powers of darkness, and bound Satan; so Joseph bore witness by love and forgiveness to his brothers, as Christ forgave humanity, and died for it and redeemed it on the Cross. And humanity heard a new language that it had not known, which is the love poured out on the Cross, love without return, and giving unto death so that humanity may change and be renewed in Christ.

81.4.0.en: 6- "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were turned from the basket.

81.4.1.en: Basket: it is the basket (sall), and its plural is baskets, in which vegetables or fruit, or earth, or sand are put...

81.4.2.en: This verse tells us about God's work with His people in Egypt, for He freed them from the forced labor with which the Egyptians forced them, for they used to carry heavy loads on their shoulders to build cities, and no longer carried the baskets full of the clay needed for making bricks, and they went out to the wilderness of Sinai and lived in freedom. So also Christ freed us from the bondage of sin, and its burdens, and its consequences by His redemption of us on the Cross

81.5.0.en: 7- Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah.

81.5.1.en: 1- God reminds His people that when it was distressed as Pharaoh and all his army pursued it, and it was hemmed in between Pharaoh's army and the Red Sea, it cried out to God and He delivered it from the hands of the Egyptians, for He sent an east wind over the Red Sea, and divided the sea, and the children of Israel crossed, when Moses struck the sea (Ex 14:21), and they reached the wilderness of Sinai, while Pharaoh and all his army were drowned in the Red Sea; so God's answer to the prayers of His people was mighty, and beyond human imagination. For God's work was hidden behind the sound of the storm, or the thunder, that divided the Red Sea; this was a miraculous work of God by which He rescued His people from death and freed them from the bondage of Egypt, so they feared God and His servant Moses.

81.5.2.en: 2- But after crossing the Red Sea God sustained the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai with water, manna and quail, and kept them from enemies, and in spite of this they doubted Him, and tempted Him at the waters of Meribah, and murmured against Him, so God was angry with them, and forbade Moses and Aaron to enter the land of Canaan.

81.5.3.en: So God punishes them for the weakness of their faith in spite of His many miracles with them.

81.5.4.en: 3- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for meditating on God's power, care, and love for His children.

81.5.5.en: Look at God's care for you throughout your life, and thank Him and praise Him until your heart is filled with joy, and God's mercies overflow upon you more and more.

81.6.0.en: (8- Hear, O my people, and I will warn thee: O Israel, if thou wilt hearken unto me;

81.6.1.en: God calls His people, who tempted Him and doubted Him at Meribah, and says to them "O my people"; to remind them that they are His children, and He is their Shepherd and their heavenly Father. And He named them "Israel" because they obey Him and hear His word. But if they disobey Him and refuse to obey Him they lose their sonship and God's care for them. So He speaks here decisively and warns them, lest they turn aside from Him to the worship of idols and all the evil lusts connected with them.

81.7.0.en: (9- There shall no strange god be in thee; neither shalt thou worship any strange god. 10- I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.

81.7.1.en: Open wide: open. God forbids His children to worship idols and all strange gods; because they believe in God their one God who is able to satisfy them with great abundance, if they open their mouths and ask Him to sustain them. For this shows their need and their faith. And here He affirms the first commandment of the Ten Commandments (Ex 20) which the people sometimes forget, as their fathers did when they worshiped idols and left God. And this happens to this day when a person relies on the powers and lusts of the world, and does not trust in God, for by this he worships other gods and forgets God.

81.8.0.en: 11- But my people would not hearken to my voice; and Israel would none of me.

81.8.1.en: 1- God speaks with sorrow about the children of His people who refused to listen to His commandments, and walked after their own thoughts and the evil thoughts of the world, so they moved away from God, although they have the name of being God's people, and they in truth reject Him; by this God does not please them, and they are not content with Him, and prefer the world and its lusts to Him. This is ingratitude, and a hardness of heart into which God's children fell, and fall to this day.

81.8.2.en: 2- This rejection of Him by God's people happened when Christ became incarnate, and preached among the Jews, His own kin, and they rejected Him and crucified Him.

81.9.0.en: 12- So I gave them up unto the hardness of their hearts, to walk in their own conspiracies.

81.9.1.en: 1- When God saw the people's insistence on evil, and the hardness of its heart, that is, its pride and refusal to hear the voice of God, He forsook them, and left them to taste the result of hardness of heart, and the evil conspiracies they devise, perhaps if they suffer from their results they will repent, and if they persist in evil like Pharaoh they will perish in the Red Sea. And God does not harden anyone's heart, but leaves him to the hardness of his heart.

81.9.2.en: 2- God left the Jews to the hardness of their hearts and their evil conspiracies, and because they said we have no king but Caesar, and crucified Christ, Caesar sent Titus the Roman commander who destroyed Jerusalem and killed the Jews in AD 70.

81.10.0.en: 13- Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! 14- I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries.

81.10.1.en: God makes clear that the cause of His people's suffering is their refusal to hear His word, and to walk in His ways, that is, His commandments. But if the people had submitted to God, He would have intervened and given them victory over their enemies quickly, and turned back upon their heads their transgression against His people. So God shows here:

81.10.2.en: 1- His concern for man's freedom, for it is necessary for his salvation..

81.10.3.en: 2- The importance of human striving "hearkened, walked" to obtain God's grace and victory.

81.10.4.en: 3- The affirmation of the well-known truth that whatever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Gal 6:7). If a person hears and walks in God's commandments he is victorious over his enemies, and if he does not hear and do, many afflictions befall him, and he should not blame God but blame himself if affliction comes upon him.

81.11.0.en: 15- The haters of the LORD should have submitted themselves unto him: but their time should have endured for ever.

81.11.1.en: 1- The wicked who hate God and refuse to obey Him, if God allows afflictions for them, and they humble themselves in them but persist in the hardness of their hearts, are cast into eternal torment, that is, they live and all their time is in torment, and if they pretend to humble themselves in order to deceive God, then of course God is not deceived and repays them for their evil with eternal torment.

81.11.2.en: 2- This verse can be interpreted in another way, namely that the haters of the Lord, if they humble themselves in repentance and return to God, then their time and their life forever will be with God in eternal happiness.

81.12.0.en: 16- He would have fed them also with the fat of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock would I have satisfied thee.

81.12.1.en: 1- God continues His speech about His children, if they obey His commandments, He pours His blessings upon them, so He gives them wheat in abundance, and it satisfies them, and he expresses that by saying "fat". And likewise He waters them with water from the rock, and because of their thirst they feel the sweetness of the water as if it were honey, that is, God sustains His people with riches and great abundance.

81.12.2.en: 2- The wheat and the rock are Christ, and He gives us His Body and His Blood, which is the fat of the wheat, and His words that water our souls and are sweet like honey.

81.12.3.en: Hold fast to God's commandments carefully at the beginning of your day; that He may lead your life in the straight way, and satisfy you, and fill your heart with peace, and so you will live in joy all the days of your life.

81.12.4.en: God the just Judge "God standeth in the congregation of God" (v. 1) Introduction:

81.12.5.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David.

81.12.6.en: 2- This psalm is among the psalms of Asaph that make clear the evils of the children of Israel, and Asaph tries to remedy them.

81.12.7.en: 3- This psalm calls the judges to judge with justice, and to do justice to the wronged, and to imitate the just God.

81.12.8.en: 4- This psalm was repeated in Jewish worship on Tuesday, as the Jewish liturgy mentions, and it is considered part of the Jewish Law because Christ referred to it and said about it to the Jews that it is written in your Law (Jn 8:17)

81.12.9.en: 5- This psalm points to the unjust judgment that the Jews passed on Christ, so it is a prophecy of what the Jews did to Christ, and in this respect it is considered one of the Messianic psalms.

81.12.10.en: 6- This psalm resembles the psalms (Ps 50, 75, 81) in that their writer is Asaph, and we also see in them God Himself speaking as a just Judge.

81.12.11.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

82.0.0.en: 1- God standeth in the congregation of God; he judgeth among the gods.

82.0.1.en: 1- God standeth in the congregation of God, and he means heaven where the angels and the saints stand before Him. And He also calls them gods: because they took of His Spirit, and He is the living God. So it is an honoring and exalting of His creation by Him. And all are subject to Him, and He judges with justice. This is an example of true judgment for the judges of the earth to follow.

82.0.2.en: 2- The congregation of God is also His people to whom He gave His commandments and His Law, and He called them the congregation of God; because they alone believe in Him in the midst of the world. And He also called them gods as a kind of honor to them, as Christ interpreted in the New Testament and declared that God calls the children of His people gods to honor them (Jn 10:34). And what may be meant by the gods is the leaders in the children of Israel.

82.0.3.en: 3- The word God here is originally, in Hebrew, Elohim, which is plural, and of course means the Holy Trinity.

82.1.0.en: 2- How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah.

82.1.2.en: 1- God rebukes the judges of the children of Israel who judge with injustice, that is, they wrong the innocent and do justice to the wicked wrongdoers, that is, He calls them to stop this unjust judgment, and to return to divine justice and upright judgment. And the act of injustice is an evil thing, but worse than it is judging with injustice; because it is the codifying and establishing of injustice, for the wicked goes further in wronging the innocent, and encourages others to fall into the sin of injustice, and the seizing of the rights of the innocent.

82.1.3.en: 2- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for a person to review himself concerning the injustice into which he falls, or the unjust judgments, that he may repent of them.

82.2.0.en: 3- Judge for the lowly and the fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. 4- Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.

82.2.1.en: 1- God requires the judges to have compassion on the weak person, such as the lowly, the orphan and the poor; for what he suffers of troubles in life is enough for him, and he needs the judge who does him justice and delivers him from the hand of the wrongdoer, so it is never right that we add to the troubles he suffers also injustice in judgment. And because the weak has no support, the judge is to be the image of God supporting this weak one and doing him justice.

82.2.2.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about Christ, who emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; that is, He had the appearance of weakness, but sadly the judges of the children of Israel, and its priests and its leaders wronged Him, and condemned Him to death, although He is righteous and holy.

82.2.3.en: Do not hasten to judge others, and do not be emotionally influenced by the words of those around you so that you honor those you love at the expense of others. Be just and speak what pleases God, and then God will also judge justly for you, and will not let people wrong you. For God has mercy on the one who has mercy on others, and forsakes the unjust, so people wrong them.

82.3.0.en: 5- They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.

82.3.1.en: 1- The unjust, wrongful judges have immersed themselves in their sins, and walk in them like one who lives in darkness, and consequently sees nothing, so he does not know and does not understand. And he is ignorant by his own will, for he refuses to be with God so as to be enlightened and judge with justice. And by this injustice with which the wicked judges rule they shake the foundations of the earth; because the wronged will cry out to the just God who founded the earth on justice, and they by their evil have changed the divine order.

82.3.2.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ whom the Jews condemned unjustly, so they crucified Him and were immersed in spiritual ignorance, so they did not know and did not understand the truth declared to them, and did not take notice when the earth shook and quaked during the crucifixion of Christ.

82.4.0.en: 6- I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.

82.4.1.en: 1- God rebukes the judges and says to them, I called you gods and sons of the Most High, that is, I raised you to a high position, so that you do the work of God, for God alone is the Judge of the whole earth: that is, I gave you the authority of judging people, and called you My sons, so how do you judge an evil judgment and wrong people and show partiality?

82.4.2.en: 2- If God honored the judges and leaders, and called them gods and sons of the Most High, then it was strange that the Jews were troubled by Christ because He declared that God is His Father. For if the judges are gods and sons of the Most High, then all the more Christ, who appeared as a teacher with authority, and a worker of miracles that no one had done with such power.

82.4.3.en: 3- Christ became incarnate to lift us up to Himself, for He took what is ours, that is, our body, and gave us what is His, that is, the blessings and works of His divinity, such as judging, and so we all became gods who offer the sacrifices of our lips before God in prayers and praises, and sons of the Most High by our spiritual conduct, and He even gave us authority over the world to judge it by our upright conduct without our knowing it, and authority also in some situations, as Moses was a god to Pharaoh (Ex 7:1), that is, he commands him with God's commands and Pharaoh submits.

82.5.0.en: 7- But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.

82.5.1.en: If the judges forget their great position that God gave them, and do not judge with truth, they die in their sins, and fall in humiliation like the leaders who fell, and died the worst of deaths, among them King Saul, upon whom an unclean spirit came and who died in the war with the Philistines, and likewise Pharaoh in the days of Moses who was drowned in the Red Sea, and also the angels who fell from heaven, that is, the demons, who were leaders of the rank of the cherubim.

82.6.0.en: 8- Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.

82.6.1.en: 1- Since the judges left the truth and passed unjust judgments, there was no solution left but for God Himself to intervene and arise, after having been silent, to judge their unjust judgments and their evils; because God is the Owner of the whole earth, so He rescues His wronged children and restores their rights to them. And the stories are many of God's intervening to do justice to the wronged, such as His bringing the children of Israel out of Egypt, and rescuing David from the hand of Saul.

82.6.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who rises from the dead after completing the redemption, and then comes to judge the whole earth on the great Day of Judgment.

82.6.3.en: Remember that you are a son of God by adoption; that you may walk well according to God's commandments, and so be a light to the world, and salt of the earth.

82.6.4.en: God destroys the wicked. A song. A psalm of Asaph. "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God) "... v. 1) Introduction:

82.6.5.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David the prophet.

82.6.7.en: a- In the days of David, and it speaks of the peoples who rose against David, but he was victorious over them by the power of God.

82.6.8.en: b- It was written in the days of David, but it is a prophecy about the peoples who attacked the king of Judah (2 Chr 20), and they are mentioned here in this psalm among the peoples hostile to God's people, and they are Moab, Edom and the children of Ammon (vv. 6, 7).

82.6.9.en: 3- This is the last of the twelve psalms that Asaph wrote, and they are (Ps 50, 73-83).

82.6.10.en: 4- We find in the title of this psalm the word song; because it is a communal lament that shows the suffering of God's people from the peoples hostile to it, and its crying out to God to rescue it from them.

82.6.11.en: 5- If the previous psalm speaks about internal troubles in the midst of God's people through unjust judgment, then this psalm speaks about external troubles from the surrounding peoples hostile to God's people.

82.6.12.en: 6- This psalm is suitable for the Church, or any human soul that the wicked or the demons attack, so it flees to God to rescue it from their conspiracies.

82.6.13.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
